summary:
Virginia stands under the United States federal framework, and the national layer of exposure is carried at country level; what follows is the state-specific position. A July 2026 national legal risk assessment places Virginia in its Low-Risk States group with Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia, and names Virginia alongside Arizona as a state that has enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies which, on that assessment, appear unlikely to extend to adults.

State civil-rights law is protective. The Virginia Values Act, passed 6 February 2020 and signed 11 April 2020, prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations and credit with effect from 1 July 2020, replacing the earlier position in which protection covered state employment only. A statute of 4 March 2020, effective 1 July 2020, allows Virginia localities to enact their own protections covering gender identity and sexual orientation, so the standards a visitor meets vary between cities and counties.

Violence against a person because of gender identity is addressed by Virginia hate-crime law under a bill signed 4 March 2020 and effective 1 July 2020. HB 2132, repealing the gay and trans panic defence, was signed by Governor Northam in March 2021 and took effect 1 July 2021, removing that line of mitigation from prosecutions over assaults on LGBTQ people.

State identity documents are comparatively open. An X gender marker has been available on Virginia driver's licences since 1 July 2020. Since 1 September 2020 changing the sex designation on a Virginia birth certificate has required only "appropriate clinical treatment," dropping the sex reassignment surgery requirement that had stood since 1979.

Facility access in Virginia schools was litigated to a favourable result for the trans student: a Gloucester County case, in which a transgender high school student was denied use of the boys' bathroom, produced a ruling that the school board had acted unlawfully, and the U.S. Supreme Court left that outcome undisturbed in 2021.

School sport is closed. In February 2025 the Virginia High School League banned transgender athletes from girls' sports, following the federal executive order on the subject.

On care, Virginia prohibits health care providers from attempting to change the gender identity of a minor.

Partner recognition is settled in practice but not fully in the state's own text. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 6 October 2014, when the Supreme Court refused appeal in Bostic v. Rainey/Schaefer and marriages began at 1 p.m. that day; the defunct statutory ban was repealed on 3 March 2020 and a codifying protection signed in March 2024 took effect 1 July 2024. The 2006 constitutional ban, however, remains on the books pending repeal resolutions approved in January 2025 and January 2026 for a voter referendum. A designated-visitor statute signed 26 March 2007 and effective 1 July 2007 extended hospital visitation rights to same-sex couples after unanimous House and Senate votes.
tangentialFactors:
The July 2026 assessment that groups Virginia among low-risk states is a comparative judgement, not a finding that no anti-trans policy exists here: the same assessment singles Virginia out with Arizona as having enacted youth-targeting measures that state-specific factors make unlikely to spread to adults. Arizona is named as the comparison, and the reasoning rests on Virginia's own political and legal conditions rather than on any difference in the text of the youth measures themselves.

Two state-level decisions point the other way. In May 2024 Governor Youngkin vetoed a bill that would have written gender identity into the statutory definition of bullying, leaving that protection out of state law. In September 2021 the Virginia Supreme Court upheld the reinstatement of a teacher suspended for refusing to use the pronouns of transgender children on Christian-belief grounds, a ruling that frames how far compelled speech protection runs in Virginia public employment.

The direction of travel at federal level has repeatedly been contested in court, and several national measures have been blocked or enjoined, so the operative position on any given national rule should be checked before travel rather than assumed from its announcement.
localsOnly:
Virginia's own protections reach residents directly: the Virginia Values Act covers gender identity in employment, housing, public accommodations and credit, and localities may add their own ordinances under the statute of 4 March 2020. Hate-crime liability and the repeal of the panic defence apply to residents and visitors alike.

Residents changing documents face a low statutory threshold. Sex designation on a birth certificate can be changed on evidence of "appropriate clinical treatment" since 1 September 2020, and an X marker has been available on driver's licences since 1 July 2020.

Family law is mixed. Virginia allows a single person to adopt with no explicit prohibition on same-sex couples, but HB 189 and SB 349, signed 9 April 2012 and effective 1 July 2012, authorise adoption agencies to refuse services on religious grounds; a February 2021 bill bars taxpayer money going to religious organisations that discriminate in adoption. Surrogacy contracts for same-sex couples were legalised by a bill passed February 2019, signed March 2019 and effective 1 July 2019.

Health and HIV policy sits partly outside protection. SB 1138, decriminalising and modernising Virginia's HIV laws, was signed 31 March 2021, while a PrEP insurance anti-discrimination bill was vetoed in March 2025. Virginia separately prohibits health providers from attempting to change the sexual orientation of a minor.
outOfScopeNotes:
The facility-ban list used by the source inventory rests on a Movement Advancement Project equality map whose cited URL now returns HTTP 404, the page having moved. Virginia's position on that state-by-state list could not be confirmed at the address held here, and remains unresolved.

The 2006 Virginia constitutional amendment banning same-sex marriage has not been repealed. Repeal resolutions were approved in January 2025 and January 2026 and now await a voter referendum, so the amendment's continued presence in the state constitution is unresolved as to timing.

An archaic Code reference defining homosexuality as sexual conduct, discovered in August 2022, is described in the sources as underpinning a criminal offence, in force since 1 July 2022, on explicit sexual conduct materials in classrooms. The precise scope of that provision and its enforcement are not sourced here.

Whether the July 2023 federal schools policy on bathroom access and pronoun usage will in fact be reversed during 2026, as the sources anticipate, is not settled in the material held for this jurisdiction.
